rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\text{Efflorescence: }Na_{2}SO_{4}\cdot10H_{2}O(s)\rightarrow Na_{2}SO_{4}(s)+10H_{2}O(g)$$
$$\text{Dehydration: }CuSO_{4}\cdot5H_{2}O(\text{blue})\rightarrow CuSO_{4}(\text{white})+5H_{2}O$$
$$n_{\text{water}}=\frac{\text{mass lost on heating}/18}{\text{moles of anhydrous salt}}$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic mean the same. ✅ Efflorescent solids *lose* water to the air, deliquescent solids *absorb water and dissolve*, hygroscopic solids *absorb water and become damp*.  ·  ❌ Deliquescence happens in any weather. ✅ It requires air humidity above the deliquescence relative humidity (≈30% for CaCl₂, ≈75% for NaCl).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: CuSO₄·5H₂O turns white on heating and blue again on adding water — the classic reversible hydration test.  ·  Deliquescence relative humidity: about 30% for CaCl₂ and 75% for NaCl.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** 2.86 g of hydrated sodium carbonate loses 1.62 g on strong heating; the anhydrous salt has M = 106 g mol⁻¹. Find n. **Solution:** anhydrous mass = 1.24 g → 0.0117 mol; water = 1.62/18 = 0.09 mol → n = 0.09/0.0117 ≈ 7.7, i.e. ≈ 8 (illustrating that heating experiments need care, since washing soda is normally the decahydrate).  ·  **Problem:** Why is CaCl₂ unsuitable for drying ammonia? **Solution:** CaCl₂ is deliquescent but forms the addition compound CaCl₂·8NH₃, so it would remove ammonia as well; conc. H₂SO₄ or quicklime is used instead.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: efflorescent, deliquescent, hygroscopic solids, crystallization (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Water of crystallisation — the concept behind the three classes  ·  Water of crystallisation is water chemically combined in a fixed stoichiometric ratio inside a crystal lattice (not merely adsorbed). Examples: CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue vitriol), Na₂CO₃·10H₂O (washing soda), Na₂SO₄·10H₂O (Glauber's salt), MgCl₂·6H₂O, CaSO₄·2H₂O (gypsum), FeSO₄·7H₂O.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Silica gel can absorb roughly 40% of its own mass of water and is regenerated by heating.  ·  answer pattern for "Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic solids; crysta…": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.

rows.text: state + explain the main idea of "Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic solids; crysta…" with one example.  ·  compare "Efflorescent" with the related idea from a neighbouring unit.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Keep one example of each class ready: efflorescent — Na₂SO₄·10H₂O; deliquescent — CaCl₂; hygroscopic — conc. H₂SO₄ or silica gel.  ·  Tie efflorescence and deliquescence to humidity: both depend on the vapour-pressure balance between hydrate and atmosphere.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Efflorescent solids  ·  Efflorescent substances lose their water of crystallisation (wholly or partly) spontaneously in dry air and crumble to a powder, because the vapour pressure of the hydrate exceeds the water-vapour pressure of the atmosphere. Examples: Na₂SO₄·10H₂O → Na₂SO₄ (white powder); Na₂CO₃·10H₂O → Na₂CO₃·H₂O; CuSO₄·5H₂O fades from blue towards pale blue/white; alum.…  ·  ### 3. Deliquescent and hygroscopic solids

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: • Crystal growth  ·  • Water of crystallization  ·  ❌ Water of crystallisation is moisture sticking to a crystal. ✅ It is chemically combined in a definite ratio and forms part of the crystal structure.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Any solid that becomes damp is deliquescent. ✅ Hygroscopic solids only become moist; deliquescent solids dissolve into a solution.  ·  ❌ Fast cooling gives the best crystals. ✅ Slow, undisturbed growth gives larger, purer crystals; rapid cooling gives many small crystals.  ·  State that crystallisation is used for purification and that slow growth yields large, pure crystals.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Distinguish efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic substances with two examples of each.  ·  Explain water of crystallisation and describe how it is determined experimentally.  ·  Why does washing soda turn to powder on standing in dry air? Write the equation.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Give four applications of crystallisation and crystal growth in industry and the laboratory.  ·  State the limitations of the efflorescent/deliquescent/hygroscopic classification.  ·  one worked example for "Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic solids; crysta…" — check units / edge cases.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: recall card: definition → formula → limit → one error to avoid.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  **Deliquescent** solids absorb moisture from the air, dissolve in it and form a saturated solution (a puddle) — CaCl₂, MgCl₂, NaOH, KOH, FeCl₃·6H₂O, ZnCl₂. **Hygroscopic** substances absorb or adsorb moisture and become damp without dissolving — concentrated H₂SO₄, P₄O₁₀, CaO (quicklime), CuO, silica gel, glycerol.…
